passage: The Class 4 room smelled of chalk and wet umbrellas. Ma'am pinned up a picture of the colony market and asked, "How many cycles are parked outside the sweet shop?" Vasudha counted. Five. She counted again, touching each one with her eyes. Five. "Four!" said Parul from the front bench, and her friends nodded. "Four, ma'am." Hands shot up for four, one after another. Last week, when Vasudha had said "Mars" instead of "Jupiter", the back row had giggled for the whole period. Her cheeks still remembered it. Slowly her hand went up with the rest. "Four," she mumbled. Ma'am turned the picture towards the window light. "Count again, everyone." Vasudha stared at the fifth cycle, half hidden behind a fruit cart, and wished her hand had stayed down.

qa.q: How many cycles did Vasudha count outside the sweet shop?
qa.a: Vasudha counted five cycles, and counted again to be sure.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha raise her hand for four even though she had counted five?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at again, because the back row had giggled the whole period when she said "Mars" last week.

qa.q: At the moment the hands went up, what choice could Vasudha have made instead?
qa.a: She could have said she counted five and pointed to the cycle behind the fruit cart, risking a few giggles but trusting her own eyes.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when ma'am asks everyone to count again?
qa.a: Parul might feel unsure and a little embarrassed, realising her quick answer made half the class copy it without checking.

grounding: A child copies the class's wrong answer although she can see the right one, because she fears being laughed at.

passage:
"Bhaiya, can I ask you something?" Aparna dropped her bag by the sofa.
"If it's quick. I've got tuition," Akash said.
"Today Sir asked which bean plant on the window was tallest. Everyone said the blue pot."
"So?"
"The red pot was taller. I could see it. It was touching the grill."
"Then why do you look like you lost a match?"
"Because I said blue too." She pulled at her sock. "Everyone was saying blue. If I said red alone, Kunal would call me Miss Red Pot for a month."
Akash sat down next to her. "Did Sir measure?"
"Tomorrow. With a scale."
"And if it's red?"
"Then I was right and I said the wrong thing." She groaned into a cushion. "Why did my mouth do that?"

qa.q: Which pot did Aparna see was taller?
qa.a: The red pot was taller; it was touching the grill.

qa.q: What was Aparna worried about when she said blue with everyone else?
qa.a: She worried that Kunal would call her Miss Red Pot for a month if she said red alone 😰

qa.q: When Sir measures tomorrow, what could Aparna choose to say?
qa.a: She could tell Sir she saw the red pot touching the grill and should have said so, a small way to stand by what she saw.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to see his sister's choice, judging from his questions?
qa.a: Akash doesn't scold; he sits beside her and asks whether Sir measured, as if helping her notice that the truth will come out anyway.

grounding: A child follows the class's answer though she can see it is wrong, because disagreeing alone risks being teased.

passage: Last year, in Class 3, our quiz team had to write one answer on the slate: how many legs does a spider have? I knew it was eight. I had counted them on the spider behind our bathroom door. But Kavitha said, "Six, obviously," and the other three said, "Yes, six." Then they all looked at me, because I was holding the chalk. My face got hot. If I said eight and was wrong, they would laugh the way they laughed when I read "island" as "is-land". So I wrote 6. We lost the point. On the way home I told Kavitha, "I knew it was eight." Kavitha stopped walking. "Then why didn't you say, Shalini?" I didn't have an answer. I still think about that chalk.

qa.q: How many legs did Shalini know a spider has?
qa.a: Shalini knew it was eight, from counting the legs on the spider behind the bathroom door.

qa.q: What was Shalini afraid of when the team looked at the chalk?
qa.a: Shalini was afraid of being laughed at for saying eight, the way the class laughed at "is-land".

qa.q: Which moment was the real choice for Shalini, and what could Shalini have done there?
qa.a: The choice came with the chalk in hand; Shalini could have said, "I counted them, it's eight," before writing anything.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel on hearing "I knew it was eight" on the walk home?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel surprised and a bit let down that a point was lost when a teammate knew the answer all along.

grounding: A child writes the group's wrong answer despite knowing the truth, because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage: Okay Deepika, you know me, Trisha, the one who hates long films. So you asked why I suddenly love that space film. Honestly? After the first watch I thought it was slow. Three hours of people staring at stars. Then on Monday in the canteen, all six of them were going, "Best film ever, the ending destroyed me." I opened my mouth to say "it dragged" and just... closed it. By evening I was thinking, maybe I was tired, maybe I missed the point. So I watched it again on the laptop, with subtitles this time. And the second half actually got me, the father's recorded messages. I cried a bit. So yes, I changed my mind. But I keep wondering: would I have given it a second chance if they hadn't all loved it? Probably not. That part bugs me.

qa.q: What did Trisha first think of the space film?
qa.a: Trisha thought it was slow, "three hours of people staring at stars".

qa.q: Why did Trisha close up in the canteen instead of saying the film dragged?
qa.a: With all six friends praising it, Trisha started to doubt that first reaction and wondered about being tired or missing the point 🤔

qa.q: Was rewatching the film a fair way to test the group's opinion, and why?
qa.a: Yes; Trisha gave it a real second look with subtitles instead of just echoing the canteen, so the new view came from Trisha's own watching.

qa.q: What would change if one friend in the canteen had said the film dragged?
qa.a: Trisha might have said "it dragged" out loud right then, since one other voice would make the first opinion feel far less risky.

grounding: A teenager faced with a group's unanimous praise of a film doubts that first view and ends up truly changing it, while wondering how much the group shaped it.

passage: My name's Tanuja. I sit right behind Nikita in Class 9, so I notice things. In July, when Neel joined, Nikita was the one who turned round to ask about his moth drawings. She said they were "actually amazing". Then the girls at her lunch table started calling him Moth Boy and rolling their eyes whenever he answered in biology. For a week Nikita still smiled at him. The next week she didn't turn round at all. Yesterday Neel showed a new drawing, someone said "so weird", and Nikita said, "Yeah, kind of." Her voice was flat, and she kept rubbing the corner of her notebook with her thumb. I can't tell if she really thinks that now or if she's just tired of being the only one. I didn't say anything either.

qa.q: What did Nikita first say about Neel's moth drawings?
qa.a: Nikita said they were "actually amazing".

qa.q: What might Nikita's flat voice and notebook-rubbing suggest when she says "Yeah, kind of"?
qa.a: They hint that Nikita may be uneasy with her own words; she might now doubt her first view, or she might just be keeping quiet to fit in.

qa.q: What small choice could Tanuja make the next time Neel shows a drawing?
qa.a: Tanuja could ask Neel about it, the way Nikita once did, which might give Nikita room to say what she really thinks.

qa.q: What is it like for Neel when Nikita, who once praised him, agrees with "so weird"?
qa.a: It likely stings more than anyone else's comment, because the one friendly voice seems to have changed sides.

grounding: An observer watches a teenager drift from her own view of a classmate to the group's scorn, unsure whether she changed her mind or only went quiet.

passage:
Monday. Hrithik handed Tejas the script for the Class 10 play, a comedy about a lost school bus. Tejas read it on the metro and snorted twice at the conductor scene. "This is really good," he texted.
Wednesday. At the cricket nets, Varun said the play was "cringe, all talking", and the other four agreed at once. Tejas bowled a wide. Maybe he'd laughed only because the train was boring. Maybe his taste was just childish. "Yeah, it's a bit long," he heard himself say.
Saturday. From the third row, Tejas bit his lip at the conductor scene so he wouldn't laugh too loudly. Afterwards the group mimicked the lines, and he stood with his hands in his pockets, saying nothing. Later, alone near the gate, he told Hrithik, "The bus bit worked," and walked off quickly.

qa.q: What was the Class 10 play about?
qa.a: It was a comedy about a lost school bus.

qa.q: What was going through Tejas's mind when he bowled a wide at the nets?
qa.a: He began doubting his own taste, wondering if he'd laughed only because the train was boring or because his taste was childish.

qa.q: On Saturday Tejas chose silence with the group and praise in private. What could he choose next time the group mocks the lines?
qa.a: He could say calmly, "I actually liked the bus bit," so his real view is heard where it counts.

qa.q: How might Hrithik take a quick, private "The bus bit worked" after the group's mimicry?
qa.a: Hrithik might feel a small lift from it, but also notice that Tejas only says it alone, which could make the praise feel thin.

grounding: Over one week a teenager goes from enjoying a script to echoing the group's scorn, and in the end keeps his real opinion quiet rather than truly changing it.

passage:
12 Aug, night
Weird thing in class today. The monitor said we should all tell ma'am our group project was fine, so we'd get the free period. It wasn't fine. Half the volcano chart was copied off the old one in the corridor. Everyone nodded. I nodded. Then Vidya, who hardly talks, said, "But isn't it kind of copied?" Just that. Silence for maybe two seconds. Then Sameer said, "Yeah, the lava part is literally the old chart." Then Ritika agreed. Then me. I even said the colours were the same. In five minutes the whole bench had turned. We're redoing the volcano on Monday. It's like everyone was waiting for one person to go first. I wish it had been me. Tomorrow I'll tell Vidya her question helped.
Pranav

qa.q: What did Vidya ask the group?
qa.a: Vidya asked, "But isn't it kind of copied?"

qa.q: What does Pranav's line "I wish it had been me" suggest about how Pranav feels?
qa.a: Pranav seems a little ashamed of just nodding and admires the nerve it took Vidya to speak first.

qa.q: Which moment turned the group, and how could Pranav use that next time?
qa.a: Vidya's single question turned it; next time Pranav could be the first to voice a doubt, or quickly back whoever does.

qa.q: What might those two seconds of silence have been like for Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya, who hardly talks, may have felt exposed and unsure whether anyone would agree, until Sameer spoke up.

grounding: A student notices that one classmate's doubt quickly lets others disagree with the group too.

passage: The local bus from the district science fair rattled past the sugarcane fields, and the Class 10 group was loud with complaints. "The judges only liked the town schools," Bablu said. "Totally," said four voices together. Suraj, squeezed by the window, remembered their water-pump model sputtering and stopping right in front of the judges. He kept quiet. Then Wasim, holding the model on his knees, said, "But our wire came loose. They saw it stop." The bus went quiet except for the engine. Then Gudiya said, "I did tape it badly." Bablu shrugged. passage:
The student council room on the third floor smelled of samosas and marker ink. Pradeep tapped the whiteboard. "So it's settled. Every first-year pays five hundred for the fest, no exceptions. All agreed?"
Eleven hands went up. Siddharth's stayed on the table.
"Half of them pay their own hostel fees," he said. "Making it compulsory isn't fair."
Every face turned. Someone laughed through their nose. Pradeep's smile thinned. "Sid, we need the money. Don't be difficult."
Siddharth felt his neck go warm. Was he being difficult? Everyone here was smart. Maybe he'd missed something in the budget. His phone buzzed: a committee friend had written, "bro why."
He swallowed. "I still think it should be optional. Please put my no in the minutes."
Afterwards, nobody passed him the samosa plate.

qa.q: How much did Pradeep want every first-year to pay?
qa.a: Every first-year was to pay five hundred for the fest, no exceptions.

qa.q: What doubts went through Siddharth's mind when every face turned to him?
qa.a: He wondered whether he really was being difficult and whether he'd missed something in the budget, since everyone else seemed smart.

qa.q: Siddharth asked for his no to go in the minutes. Why was that a meaningful choice?
qa.a: It kept his objection on record calmly, so the fairness question stays visible even though he lost the vote.

qa.q: How might a first-year who pays their own hostel fees see Siddharth's stand if they heard about it?
qa.a: They might feel that at least one council member noticed people like them, and be grateful even though the vote didn't change.

grounding: A young adult who alone disagrees in a council meeting faces stares, pressure and self-doubt, and pays a small social price for holding his view.

passage:
It's been a month, and I still remember the heat in my ears. Our sociology group had to run a survey. We got eighty-seven responses. Jatin wanted to write "over two hundred" on the slide. "Nobody checks," he said, and the other three laughed and agreed. I said, "I'm not presenting a number we made up." Four people looked at me like I'd switched off the wifi. For two days the group chat went silent whenever I posted. I lay awake thinking maybe I was being a goody-goody, maybe everyone rounds up. Then the professor asked every group to upload raw data. Jatin messaged me: "ok fine, 87." No thanks, no sorry. Being right didn't feel like winning. It felt like paying a small bill, one I'd pay again.
Amandeep

qa.q: How many survey responses did the group actually get?
qa.a: They got eighty-seven responses.

qa.q: What was Amandeep worried about while lying awake after the meeting?
qa.a: Amandeep wondered about being a goody-goody, thinking that maybe everyone rounds up numbers.

qa.q: Looking back, which moment was the real choice, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Saying "I'm not presenting a number we made up" to four laughing teammates was the choice; it cost two days of a silent group chat.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel typing "ok fine, 87"?
qa.a: Jatin may feel embarrassed at being caught by the raw-data rule, which could explain why there is no thanks or sorry.

grounding: A young adult who stands alone against a group's plan to inflate numbers feels stares and doubt, and finds that being right still carries a social cost.

passage: I'm Vidya, and I've sat across from Raghav in the Monday planning meeting for a year. This Monday the whole team was ready to promise the client the app update by the fifteenth. Our manager asked, "Everyone fine with that?" and people nodded. Raghav didn't nod. He opened his laptop, scrolled for a minute, and turned the screen round. "I could be wrong," he said, "but last time the testing alone took nine days. If we start on the fifth, how do we fit it?" Nobody answered at first. Then the manager asked him to walk through the numbers. Halfway through, Meenal pointed out that two tests could run at the same time, and Raghav said, "Oh, good, that changes it." We settled on the eighteenth. I can't say if he was nervous. His voice was steady; his pen kept clicking.

qa.q: How long did the testing take last time, according to Raghav?
qa.a: Raghav said the testing alone took nine days last time.

qa.q: What might Raghav's clicking pen suggest, even though his voice was steady?
qa.a: It might suggest he felt nervous about disagreeing with the whole team, though Vidya can't be sure.

qa.q: Which of Raghav's choices opened the discussion instead of starting a fight?
qa.a: He framed his doubt as a question backed by numbers, "how do we fit it?", rather than simply declaring the date wrong.

qa.q: How might Meenal have felt when Raghav said, "Oh, good, that changes it"?
qa.a: Meenal likely felt heard and respected, since Raghav took the correction instead of defending his first point.

grounding: A colleague watches a young professional check his reasoning, disagree politely with evidence and a question, and stay open to being corrected.

passage:
Tuesday. Everyone in the design team loved the new printing vendor's samples. Sonali did too, but last year's delivery dates didn't match what the vendor had promised. That evening she checked the old invoices twice, then asked her flatmate to poke holes in her logic.
Thursday. At the review, Saurabh said, "So we sign today?" Sonali raised her hand. "Before we do, can I share one thing? I might have missed something." She showed three late deliveries. "Is there a reason we're not worried about these?" Saurabh frowned, then said, "Fair question."
Next Monday. On a call, the vendor explained that one delay had been caused by a flood. Sonali nodded. "Then that one doesn't count. I was wrong there." The team agreed on a small trial order first.

qa.a: Saurabh may see her as someone whose objections are worth hearing, because she asked instead of attacking and conceded when new facts came.

passage: Sit, Eshaan. You asked how to disagree with your boss without losing your job. Your Chinmay mama was twenty-five once, you know, a junior in the roads department. passage:

passage: Imran, come, sit. You fought with your sister again? Your Usha aunty was nine once, you know, and my little sister Leela and I quarrelled every single day. One morning she cut my red ribbon to make a doll's scarf. I screamed and told her she was no sister of mine. That same evening, at the village pump, two older boys splashed her and pulled her plait until she cried. I didn't think at all. I marched over with my bucket and said, "Touch her again and I'll tell the whole school, and your mothers." My knees were knocking. They went. Leela held my hand all the way home, ribbon forgotten. That is how it is, beta. You can be angry with your own and still stand in front of them.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the bus shelter, and the school van was already twenty minutes late. Omkar, ten, stood as far as he could from his brother Tushar. "Wet baby," he sneered. Tushar's lip wobbled. Omkar crossed the shelter in three steps. "Stop it. He's my brother." The older boy was a head taller. Omkar didn't move, even as water soaked his socks. When the van finally splashed up, Omkar pushed Tushar in first and sat beside him, still not talking, but shoulder to shoulder.

Dear Swati didi,
Mummy says your hostel fee is paid for this term. Good. I'm glad, really.
I want to tell you something, though, and you're the only one I can tell. The Class 10 trip to the hills was the same week the fee was due. I told Mummy I didn't want to go. I said I'd rather study. That wasn't true. Everyone came back with photos of snow, and Rhea brought me a small wooden bear. I kept it on my desk, then put it in a drawer because it made me a bit angry every time I saw it.
I'm not angry at you. I'm proud you're the first one in our family at college. Both things are in me at once, and I don't know where to put them.
Send me a photo of your hostel room?
Love,
Neelam

passage: By August, Layla had worked eleven weeks at the bakery by the harbour, long enough to know who closed up properly. Ana did: counted the till, wiped the ovens, never left early. Ana just nodded and went back to the dough. Later the owner told Layla, a little embarrassed, "His mother helped me open this place. He's practically family." Layla could picture that, and it softened her; she'd want to help someone like that too. But walking home she kept seeing Ana's floury hands, and eleven weeks of good work that hadn't counted.

Dear Kiran,
You asked how the internship at the insurance office is going. Mostly fine. But something happened that I can't stop thinking about.
They were hiring one junior clerk. Two people interviewed: a woman from the evening college who answered every question sharply, and Harpreet veerji, whose family and mine have celebrated every Lohri together since before I was born. The branch head is his father's old friend. Harpreet got the job the same afternoon.
I was happy for him for about ten minutes. I even texted Mum. Then I saw the other candidate at the bus stop, reading her notes again. She didn't know yet.
I understand why it happened. If it were my own brother, would I want someone to help? Probably yes. That's what bothers me.
Write back and tell me what you'd have done.
Baljeet

passage: Rafael turned up at Ingrid's flat with two suitcases and a parking fine. His lease had ended and his new job didn't start for three weeks. "You're my favourite cousin," he said. "You work at the council office. Just make it disappear." Ingrid put down her coffee. "I'll help you pay it bit by bit if you want. I won't make it disappear." "It's nothing to them!" "It's my job, and it's the same rule for everyone who parks there." Rafael sulked through dinner. She passed him the bread anyway. "I love you, and I'm not doing that. Both are true."

Sumit stepped out into the corridor with her. "Bua, I spent last Sunday fixing this file with you, and I'll come again if anything's missing. But I can't put it on top."

Kamal,
I've transferred the money for your driving course, and I've kept Saturday afternoon free to help you practise for the interview. Please stop thanking me; you're my little brother, that's the job.
